newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Spending cuts to create "realistic" Russia budget.
newsitem.headline: Spending cuts to create "realistic" Russia budget.

text.p: Spending cuts promised by First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais will create a "realistic" Russian budget for the first time since economic reforms began, an economist working with the Russian finance ministry said.

Jochen Wermuth, head of the Finance Ministry's Economic Expert Group, said the cuts -- known as sequestration -- would mean that revenues made up about 11 percent of gross domestic product, compared with expenditure of 17 percent of GDP.
"The revenues are now a realistic forecast, instead of these loony figures we had before. The budget was not realistic last year or in 1992-95," he told Reuters.

"It is a very difficult step, but it is good that they have taken it. Russia will come out with some form of law on sequestration... The government is finally getting honest. This is quite an important signal."

Wermuth said expenditure accounting for two percent of GDP was being used to pay wage and pension arrears in 1997 -- which he said was similar to the two percent used in the first half of 1996 to fund President Boris Yeltsin's re-election campaign.
Ministers say low tax revenues and wage and pension arrears are Russia's most pressing economic problems.
But Wermuth said revenues -- just 59 percent of planned levels in the first quarter -- were in line with last year's revenues, which meant spending could be the same as well.

"If you compare spending to the planned budget, then lots of things get cut. if you compare it to de facto 1996, it will be very similar, in the sense that all protected items will be covered and others will get two percent less of GDP," he said.

The Russian budget, approved after prolonged and angry debates in the State Duma lower house of parliament, includes so-called protected items like health, education and the military where spending cannot be cut.
But the low revenues mean new plans must be drawn up, cutting spending across the board and finding additional ways to bring in cash.
Reform chief Anatoly Chubais admitted on Thursday that the budget was unrealistic. He said the government would raise an extra $5 billion with privatisation and precious metals sales.
Parliamentary sources said the government would present its new spending plans to parliament on May 21, a delay of some four weeks from the April 23 date originally scheduled.
Deputies have already indicated that the plans will face a rough ride in the Duma, which is dominated by communists and other conservatives.

Chubais also said that shortages of budget cash meant the Russian government would have to use "unusual measures" such as guaranteed bank loans to the farm sector to finance the cash-starved spring sowing campaign.
Wermuth said this should not be a burden on the budget if the figures involved were less than one trillion roubles.
